1: Recognising the name is not enough: notice how Ko identifies who the bird is.
2: He introduces a kind of thing. Compare ‘a kākāpō’ with naming a particular bird.
3: Wellington names the place; Nō supplies the relationship ‘from’. Listen for both.
4: The location comes first. Resist reading the Māori in English word order.
5: Keep ‘above’ and the thing it is above together in meaning, even with the bird between them.
6: Notice the whole E rua pattern, not just the number rua.
7: Compare Tokorua with E rua. The counting expression changes, not just the thing being counted.
10: This denies an identity or category, rather than saying an action did not happen.
11: The owner comes first here. Do not mistake the first noun for the thing that belongs to it.
12: Compare Nō with Nā. The English ‘belongs to’ hides a distinction visible in Māori.
13: ‘For the bird’ is different from ‘belongs to the bird’. The small opening word carries that change.
14: Compare this with Mā: similar English wording can conceal different Māori choices.
15: Track what Ehara denies: the ownership relationship, not the existence of the seed.
16: Keep the negative and the ownership expression together when interpreting the sentence.
17: The sentence denies who something is for. It is not a command to stop an action.
18: Listen for both the negative and Mō; knowing the two nouns will not reveal this relationship.
19: Notice ake and the comparison phrase. Two familiar nouns alone do not tell you which is bigger.
20: The first I places the action in the past; the later i marks its object. The adjectives follow their nouns.
21: Compare ‘has eaten’ with ‘ate’. Kua adds a different view of the same action.
22: Keep Kei te with the verb. Hearing only kai loses the ‘is eating’ part.
23: E and ana sit on opposite sides of the verb. Learn to hear them as one pattern.
24: In this example, Ka changes the observation to ‘will eat’; the verb itself stays the same.
25: ‘Should eat’ is not ‘will eat’. Listen for Me rather than guessing from the action word.
26: The opening marker changes how the action is presented. Compare ‘is to eat’ with ‘is eating’.
27: The small ai after the verb presents this as what the bird habitually does: it always chases the green bird.
28: An action that did not happen
Kāore and the later verb phrase work together. Do not stop interpreting once you recognise kai.
29: Compare ‘was not eating’ with ‘did not eat’. The extra te changes the pattern to notice.
30: An action that will not happen
Compare the e after the subject with i in the past-negative example.
31: ‘Not yet’ leaves room for the action to happen later. Hear anō as part of the negative pattern.
32: The doer is brought forward. Follow the markers instead of assuming ordinary action-first order.
33: The sentence highlights who went; the destination is a different role, introduced by ki.
34: Compare Mā with Nā in the past example. The emphasis stays on the doer while the time changes.
35: Keep the highlighted doer separate from the destination, even though both are noun phrases.
36: This denies that it was the red bird. It does not simply say nobody chased the green bird.
37: The negative targets the highlighted doer, not necessarily the whole event.
38: Track both the negative and Mā: who will do it is the focus of this example.
39: Compare with the positive version. A small added negative changes the claim about the doer.
40: Follow the roles through the whole sentence: the doer, the thing affected, and the action are separate parts.
41: ‘Can fly’ describes ability, not a promise that flying will happen. Keep the destination separate.
42: Kāore e taea makes the ability negative. The action still comes late in this transitive pattern.
43: Kāore e taea expresses inability here; it is a statement, not a question.
44: The question asks for a reason. Notice He aha and the later ai, not only the past action.
45: Compare this ongoing-action question with ‘Why did it happen?’ Keep the extra te audible.
46: The reason question stays, but the action marker changes. Do not translate every version as past.
47: Keep i kore ai together before the action phrase; ai is not attached to kai in this negative pattern.
48: Listen for both i kore ai and the ongoing action phrase. The question is about non-occurrence now.
49: The negative reason phrase and the following e each contribute meaning. Neither is just decoration.
50: Nōnahea asks about time, not the reason. Compare it with the He aha questions.
51: Compare Āhea with Nōnahea. The opening question word helps distinguish the two time perspectives.
52: This introduces a condition, not a claim that the action happened. Expect a consequence to follow.
53: Keep the ‘if’ meaning while recognising the familiar action pattern inside the condition.
54: Read Ki te as the opening conditional pattern here, not as a destination phrase.
55: The action from the other side
The affected thing comes forward. Use the passive verb and e to find who actually did it.
56: Notice the state of the seeds. In this reviewed example, i introduces the doer rather than a victim.
57: This is an instruction, not a report of an event. Notice the passive form of the verb.
58: The destination follows ki. It is not an object being acted on.
59: Kaua e tells someone not to act. Compare it with Kāore reporting that an action did not happen.
60: ‘Stop eating’ assumes an activity to stop. Keep te kai as the verbal expression in this example.
61: Kia presents what is wanted here, rather than reporting what is already true.
62: Learn the complete Kotahi expression rather than trying to build it by copying E rua word for word.
63: The negative concerns there being any birds at all, not what a bird did.
64: Mēnā makes the action conditional. Understanding the familiar nouns and verb is only half the sentence.
